content.title: What is Insertion?
content.description: Insertion is the process of adding a new node into a Linked List while maintaining the connections between existing nodes.

content.content: One of the biggest advantages of Linked Lists is efficient insertion. Unlike arrays, Linked Lists do not require shifting elements when inserting new data.

content.title: Why Linked Lists Are Powerful
content.content: Insertion can often be performed in O(1) time by simply updating pointers.
Why Insertions Matter
Applications frequently require adding new data dynamically. Linked Lists allow insertion without reallocating memory or shifting existing elements.
Types of Insertion Operations

items.question: Insertion at Beginning
items.answer: Add a node before the Head.

items.question: Insertion at End
items.answer: Add a node after the last node.

items.question: Insertion After a Given Node
items.answer: Add a node directly after a known node.

content.content: Insertion at the Beginning
Insertion at the beginning is one of the fastest Linked List operations because only the Head pointer must be updated.
Insertion at the End
Insertion at the end requires locating the last node and updating its next pointer.

content.title: Important Observation
content.content: Without a Tail pointer, insertion at the end requires traversal.
Insertion at a Specific Position
Sometimes a node must be inserted at a particular index inside the Linked List.

content.title: Insertion at Position Steps
steps: Point New Node to Next Node

content.title: Link Adjustment
content.description: The new node must be connected before breaking the existing link.

content.content: Insertion After a Given Node
If a reference to a node is already available, insertion can be performed directly after it.

content.title: Efficiency
content.content: If the target node is already known, insertion can be completed in O(1) time.
Pointer Visualization

content.title: Golden Rule
content.description: Always preserve existing links before updating pointers.

content.content: Insertion in Empty Linked List
When the Linked List is empty, the inserted node becomes the Head node.

content.title: Special Case
content.content: Always check whether the Linked List is empty before performing insertion.
Common Insertion Mistakes

items.question: Losing References
items.answer: Updating pointers in the wrong order can disconnect nodes.

items.question: Forgetting NULL Checks
items.answer: Always verify nodes exist before accessing pointers.

items.question: Incorrect Position Calculation
items.answer: Traversal count errors can place nodes incorrectly.

content.title: Interview Tip
content.content: Most interview questions focus on pointer manipulation. Always explain how links are updated before discussing code.

content.title: Interview Insight
content.description: Insertion operations test a candidate's understanding of memory references and pointer management more than algorithmic complexity.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: Insertion adds a new node to the Linked List.
End insertion requires traversal without a Tail pointer.
Position insertion requires finding the previous node.
Insertion is a major Linked List advantage.
